{
  "answer_markdown": "## Short answer
No — do not raise Meta spend on the current reported ROAS. The platform number improved, but Shopify results fell, Meta’s reported purchase value now exceeds total Shopify net product revenue, and a simple new-customer ceiling test puts Meta’s maximum plausible new-customer MER below the Daypack 18L break-even ROAS. This is a reconciliation problem, not a scale signal.

## Reconcile the numbers

| Metric | Previous 30d | Current 30d | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Shopify sessions | 20,000 | 25,000 | +25.0% |
| Shopify orders | 600 | 500 | -16.7% |
| Net product revenue | $54,000 | $45,000 | -16.7% |
| AOV | $90 | $90 | 0% |
| Conversion rate | 3.0% | 2.0% | -1.0 pp |
| Mobile CVR | 2.67% | 1.50% | -1.17 pp |
| Desktop CVR | 4.00% | 4.00% | 0 pp |
| Add-to-cart sessions | 2,000 | 2,000 | 0% |
| Checkout-started sessions | 1,200 | 1,000 | -16.7% |
| Meta spend | $18,000 | $22,000 | +22.2% |
| Meta reported value | $54,000 | $70,400 | +30.4% |
| Meta reported ROAS | 3.00 | 3.20 | +0.20 |
| Blended Shopify/Meta MER | 3.00 | 2.05 | -0.95 |
| Meta CPM | $12 | $15 | +25.0% |
| Meta link CTR | 1.5% | 1.2% | -0.3 pp |
| Klaviyo attributed revenue | — | $14,000 | — |

Arithmetic: current Meta ROAS = $70,400 ÷ $22,000 = 3.20. Current blended Shopify/Meta MER = $45,000 ÷ $22,000 = 2.05. Previous = $54,000 ÷ $18,000 = 3.00. So the business-level revenue per Meta dollar fell while the platform-reported ROAS rose.

Meta’s current reported value is 156% of total Shopify net product revenue: $70,400 ÷ $45,000 = 1.564, or $25,400 more than Shopify recorded. Adding Klaviyo’s reported $14,000 gives $84,400 of platform-attributed revenue against $45,000 of Shopify revenue — 187.6% of the actual base. These systems overlap, so they are not additive, but the gross inflation is the key warning.

## New-customer ceiling test
Current Shopify net revenue is $45,000. Current new-customer share is 72%, so new-customer revenue is $45,000 × 0.72 = $32,400. If every single new-customer dollar were credited to Meta — an impossible best case — Meta’s new-customer MER would be $32,400 ÷ $22,000 = 1.47. Meta reports 3.20, which is 2.2× that ceiling.

Daypack 18L break-even: $80 price − $28 COGS − $2 pick/pack − $8 merchant shipping − $2.40 payment fee (3% × $80) = $39.60 contribution. Margin = 49.5%. Break-even ROAS on net product revenue = 1 ÷ 0.495 = 2.02. The new-customer ceiling of 1.47 is below break-even. Even the blended 2.05 is only at break-even, and that assumes all Shopify revenue was Meta-driven, which it is not.

## Klaviyo context
Klaviyo’s $14,000 is 31.1% of Shopify revenue. Its 5-day click + 5-day open window overlaps Meta and Shopify, and there is no holdout. It cannot be added to Meta to prove incremental performance. If Klaviyo were incremental, Meta’s already-generous new-customer ceiling would fall further: ($32,400 − $14,000) ÷ $22,000 = 0.84. That subtraction is not valid because of overlap, but it shows how contested the Meta number is.

## What can be concluded
- Meta spend rose 22.2%, and Meta reported purchase value rose 30.4%, so platform-reported ROAS improved from 3.00 to 3.20.
- Shopify orders and revenue fell, so the business-level result worsened.
- Meta is buying more expensive, lower-CTR traffic: CPM +25%, link CTR -20%.
- Mobile conversion fell from 2.67% to 1.50% while desktop held at 4.00%; traffic growth came from mobile sessions. That is an observation, not proof that Meta caused the decline.
- Meta’s reported value exceeding total Shopify revenue is a strong signal of over-attribution, overlapping credit, or definition mismatch.

## What cannot be concluded
- We cannot conclude Meta drove incremental new-customer revenue or that its ROAS is real. There is no incremental lift study, no holdout, and no reconciled attribution.
- We cannot add Meta and Klaviyo attributed revenue to Shopify. They overlap.
- We cannot compute true CAC, incremental ROAS, or cohort contribution LTV from the supplied data.
- We cannot conclude the “laptop-fit comparison” creative is a scalable winner; it had higher CTR in a small test, but conversion sample was not supplied.
- We cannot attribute the mobile conversion drop to Meta alone; PDP clarity, delivery-date anxiety, 15-inch laptop-fit questions, and waterproof confusion are plausible friction themes, but no field speed or session-recording data exists.

## Recommended next steps within constraints
1. Change Meta reporting only to 7-day click / 1-day engaged, or 7-day click only, and re-read ROAS. Do not change delivery yet. Verify current interface labels.
2. Pull Meta new-vs-existing audience breakdown and frequency. Recalculate ROAS on the new-audience segment only. If much spend lands on existing customers, do not scale.
3. Use DAY18 new-customer sales as the cleanest readout. Confirm
